document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
) 
Exploring The Current State of  
 
)  
 Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
PJM Governance 
 
 
 
) 
 
 
 
  
 
COMMENTS OF MAREC ACTION AND  
THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION  
 
Pursuant to the July 30, 2026 notice inviting comments,1 MAREC Action2 and the Solar 
Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)3 submit these recommended governance reforms for the 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) Board and stakeholder process. 
MAREC Action and SEIA represent developers of all different sizes and business 
models. These run the gamut from small rooftop solar installers to large multinational 
corporations. It includes both public and private companies, some are North American 
subsidiaries of international companies, some are owned by pension funds or private equity 
funds, are smaller owner-operated businesses. They have a variety of business models. Some are 
owner-operators, others build and sell projects, while others build projects under contract to 
other entities. But they all have something in common—they want to get generation projects 
built in the PJM region to serve the growing load.  
Many of these developers represented by MAREC Action and SEIA have project 
development experience outside of PJM, both in other Regional Transmission Organization 
(“RTO”) markets and in non-RTO regions. Some, that are subsidiaries of international 
 
1 Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment, Docket No. AD26-7 (July 30, 2026). 
2 MAREC Action (informally, “Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition”) is a coalition of over 40 utility-scale 
solar, wind, and battery storage developers and manufacturers dedicated to the growth and development of 
renewable energy across the PJM grid region. The views and opinions expressed in this filing do not necessarily 
reflect the official position of each individual member of MAREC Action. 
3 The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar 
industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.

2 
 
companies, also have project development experience outside the US. Many are actively 
involved in the stakeholder processes in other regions and have first-hand experience in what 
works well and what needs improvement. The recommendations below are informed by these 
diverse business models and stakeholder experiences.4 
As the Commission, PJM, and stakeholders begin the arbitration process, MAREC Action 
and SEIA request that these recommendations are considered and incorporated into the final 
reforms. 
 
I. 
Stakeholders need insight into Board direction and decisions 
Insight into Board decisions is sorely lacking in PJM. Stakeholders have very little 
knowledge of how and why the Board acts as it does s. Many decisions in the recent past seem to 
be rushed attempts to put out fires rather than deliberate well-planned decisions that would move 
PJM into the future. Short-term fixes seem to have become the norm. PJM has jumped from 
emergency to emergency, establishing reforms that are simultaneously rushed and too late. This 
can be seen in the multiple uses of the Critical Issues Fast Path Process over the last few years 
that have resulted in some major changes to the PJM markets with very little insight into how the 
Board arrived at those decisions.   
Meanwhile, reforms that could address many of the fundamental problems, such as 
comprehensive transmission and generation interconnection planning, and energy and capacity 
market reforms, have fallen by the wayside. For years, as we watched other regions move to 
more granular markets, stakeholders have told themselves, “this is the year PJM will enact 
 
4 MAREC Action and SEIA’s silence on a particular issue does not necessarily represent internal disagreement, 
acquiescence to the status quo, or agreement with any particular position taken in this proceeding.

3 
 
comprehensive market reforms that address systemic issues.” However, it seems these remain on 
the side-lines or are bogged down in endless debates in the stakeholder process. MAREC Action 
and SEIA applaud PJM for their recent commitment to exploring capacity market reforms,5 but 
we urge PJM to ensure that this is not an empty commitment. As PJM pursues these reforms, it 
must do so with the input of its stakeholders and it must be transparent in its choices. 
A. 
Recommendation: The Board and PJM should work with stakeholders to 
identify initiatives and develop an annual priorities plan. 
Identifying initiatives and then setting annual priorities is fundamental to any 
organization. The Board and PJM staff need to work with stakeholders to identify critical needs 
and then prioritize the work. PJM has conducted some of this type of priority planning in the past 
but then failed to hold to those priorities. To be fair, the constant putting out of fires has 
interfered with this. However, if many of the long-time fundamental issues were identified 
earlier and worked on more holistically, the fires would not be as critical. Addressing these 
emergency needs must be done in the context of longer-term priorities. PJM just released a new 
strategy document, Shaping a Powerful Change, PJM Five-Year Strategy.6 While this is a start, 
the document is high-level and lacking in actionable elements. We hope that more is to come in 
the form of an actual roadmap and workplan outlining the detailed policies and procedures that 
should be prioritized and worked.  
PJM need only look to its fellow Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs) to see 
good examples of annual prioritization exercises and plan development. In the Midcontinent 
 
5 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Powering Reliability Through Market Design, May 6, 2026, 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-
through-market-design.pdf.  
6 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Shaping a Power Change, PJM Five-Year Strategy, August 2026. 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260819-shaping-a-powerful-
change-pjm-five-year-strategy.pdf

4 
 
Independent System Operating, Inc. (MISO), Reliability Imperatives set the direction on an 
annual basis. “MISO, its members, and its states have a shared responsibility to address the 
urgent and complex challenges facing the electric grid. We call this the Reliability Imperative.”7 
The Reliability Imperative Report (last updated in February 2026) is a living document created in 
collaboration with all stakeholders to outline strategic priorities. The report evolves, assesses, 
and responds to the Reliability Imperative.8 
Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) has a Strategic Plan and Strategic Roadmap. The first 
strategic plan was launched in 2021, Aspire 2026.9 It was a five-year plan covering 2021-2026 
that “sought to strengthen regional reliability, advance market development, and prepare its 
region and business for the challenges and opportunities that lay ahead.”10 Earlier this year, SPP 
released the 2027-2031 Strategic Plan,11 which will define SPP’s activities over the next five 
year. Complementary to, and aligned with, the Strategic Plan is the Strategic Roadmap that 
outlines the activities required to meet the goals of the Strategic Plan.12 
Every year starting in January, the California Independent System Operator, Corp. 
(CAISO) conducts an Annual Policy Initiatives Catalog and Roadmap Development Process that 
“prioritizes and sequences market design enhancements by soliciting policy initiative proposals 
from stakeholders, assessing stakeholder support for proposed policy initiatives, and 
 
7 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Corporate Strategy, Reliability Imperative, 
https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/MISO_Strategy/.  
8 MISO, 2026 Reliability Imperative Report, February 2026, 
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/2026%20Reliability%20Imperative%20Report744320.pdf.  
9 See SPP, Aspire 2026 July 14, 2021, https://www.spp.org/documents/65050/spp%20strategic%20plan%202021-
2026.pdf. 
10 SPP, Strategic Plan, https://www.spp.org/about-us/strategic-plan/.  
11 See SPP, Powering Progress Forward, https://www.spp.org/documents/76666/2027-
2031%20strategic%20plan.pdf. 
12 SPP, Roadmap, https://www.spp.org/stakeholder-center/spp-roadmap/.

5 
 
documenting a work plan, called the roadmap, for future policy initiatives.”13 This year, CAISO 
bifurcated its annual stakeholder process to create the 2026 Market Policy Catalog and 
Roadmap14 and the 2026 Infrastructure Policy Catalog and Roadmap.15 These tracks prioritize 
and sequence 2027-2029 market design and transmission enhancements based on stakeholder 
proposals and CAISO strategic goals. 
B. 
Improvements to Board Transparency 
1. 
Recommendation: The Board should host open meetings, publish roll 
call votes, and issue decisional memos with their directives. 
PJM’s Board meetings are closed. Cursory, high-level minutes of those meetings are 
provided after the Board meetings. This is not indicative of good governance. Transparency 
measures must be implemented to ensure that Members, States, and other stakeholders can 
engage effectively and meaningfully with the PJM Board. Essential transparency measures 
include open Board meetings, published roll call Board votes, detailed Board meetings minutes 
that show the rationale for the Board’s vote, and decisional memos between the Board and PJM 
Staff. 
2. 
Recommendation: Board members should schedule regular meetings 
with Members, States, and Stakeholders. 
Access to the Board would be another important step towards good governance. 
Although the Board meets with the Liaison Committee and has private meetings with the 
Organization of PJM States, Inc. (“OPSI”) Board three times a year, these meetings are not 
 
13 CAISO 2026 Annual Policy Initiatives Catalog and Roadmap Development Process, 
https://www.caiso.com/notices/2026-annual-policy-initiatives-catalog-and-roadmap-development-process--call-on-
1-15-26.  
14 Id. 
15 CAISO, 2026 Infrastructure Policy Catalog and Roadmap Process, 
https://stakeholdercenter.caiso.com/RecurringStakeholderProcesses/2026-Infrastructure-policy-catalog-and-
roadmap-process.

6 
 
enough. The Board should schedule regular meetings with Members, States, and Stakeholders, 
along with detailed minutes of the meetings. Transparency of Board actions, as described above, 
coupled with access to the Board, will more closely align accountability with responsibility. 
II. 
Recommendation: Consider moving to an advisory voting system. 
As stated repeatedly throughout this proceeding, the PJM stakeholder process has become 
slow and unfocused. There are tools to speed up the process, like the Critical Issue Fast Path 
which is used to address “time-constrained major issues or existing work efforts that have not 
achieved, or are unlikely to achieve, consensus.”16 But, as PJM noted in its pre-conference 
comments, the CIFP has recently resulted in failures to achieve any sort of consensus in a timely 
manner.17 Such failures will likely continue to happen, since controversial issues cannot move 
forward without frustrating one group or another. PJM leadership and the Board must be 
empowered to make difficult decisions. Member advisory voting grants that power. 
As a practical matter, moving to an advisory voting structure does not change the status 
quo. According to PJM, “PJM and its stakeholders reach consensus on the majority of issues 
considered.”18 And with respect to the CIFP process, the votes are already advisory.19 The 
recommendations made in this proceeding will likely lead to more supported, and sustainable, 
proposals in the longer-term. However, in the near-term, PJM will be forced to make hard 
decisions, and it must have the ability to act quickly and decisively. By moving to a member 
 
16 PJM Manual 34, Sec. 8.6.4, 
https://www.pjm.com/pjmfiles/directory/manuals/m34/index.html#Sections/Section_8_Consensus_Based_Issue_Res
olution_at_the_Standing_Committee_Level_other_than_the_Senior_Standing_Committees.html. 
17 See PJM Comments at 4; see also Jacob Finkle comments calling the recent CIFP a failure. 
18 Prefiled Statement for Panelists from PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., for the PJM Governance and Stakeholder 
Reforms Technical Conference at 1 (“PJM Comments”). 
19 PJM Manual 34, Sec. 8.6.4, 
https://www.pjm.com/pjmfiles/directory/manuals/m34/index.html#Sections/Section_8_Consensus_Based_Issue_Res
olution_at_the_Standing_Committee_Level_other_than_the_Senior_Standing_Committees.html.

7 
 
advisory voting, PJM leadership and the Board can move forward without being bogged down 
by a drawn out, and as of recently, often-failing stakeholder process. 
This advisory structure should not be viewed in isolation; it is one component of a 
broader set of reforms needed to make PJM’s stakeholder process more effective and responsive 
and if this change is made it needs to be combined with the reforms discussed below. 
III. 
The PJM stakeholder process is in dire need of reform. 
Over the years, the process has become slow, unfocused,20 and polarizing.21 The 
recommendations below would help create a stakeholder process that will ensure robust 
proposals that address concerns by different sectors and allow PJM to move quickly to address 
emerging issues. 
A. 
Recommendation: At beginning of stakeholder process, PJM staff should 
establish the objectives any proposed solution must satisfy and what solutions 
cannot be entertained. 
MAREC Action and SEIA appreciate that PJM leadership welcomes multiple viewpoints 
throughout the stakeholder process. Hearing from a wide range of stakeholders can create 
reforms that accomplish PJM’s goals while also reflecting operational realities and market needs. 
But PJM and its stakeholders should not be spending hours discussing proposals that have 
elements that cannot be implemented because they are operationally infeasible. To create 
meaningful reforms, PJM needs to refocus stakeholders on what solutions can be pursued. 
At the start of each stakeholder process, PJM must clearly define the problem they are 
seeking to solve, the timeframe for action, and any operational limitations that may limit 
solutions. PJM issue charges and problem statements do define the problem, set the timing, and 
 
20 Pre-filed Statement of Glen Thomas, President of PJM Power Providers Group at 4 (P3 Comments). 
21 PJM Comments at 3.

8 
 
define what is out of scope.22 However, the issue charge could be more precise. Instead of 
“intermediate,” “near term,” and “far term,” timelines should identify when the proposal would 
be filed at the Commission or when an appropriate Manual change will be made, such as “Q1 
2027,” or “before December 31, 2026.” Further, while issue charges do outline what is “out of 
scope” in a proceeding, they do not reflect when a potential solution that is in scope may not be 
available because of operational limitations. To the extent possible, PJM should identify these 
issues upfront. If PJM cannot, then it must have discretion to edit proposals throughout the 
stakeholder process, by removing part of, or the entire proposal, from consideration. PJM staff 
must be able to state that a particular proposal is not operational and thus cannot be 
implemented. 
A successful stakeholder process is one that sets forward clear guidelines earlier in the 
process and constant editing during the process. PJM must be clear in what it needs to 
accomplish, what it can do to meet those goals, and acknowledge where it does not have 
sufficient knowledge about a problem or market segment. 
 
B. 
Recommendation: PJM should provide a pathway for written comments and 
questions on proposals that are publicly posted to a central location.  
Several panelists noted in their pre-filed comments that stakeholder meetings are 
sometimes derailed for multiple hours by a small number of participants engaging in extended, 
unfocused discussion.23 In order to get in feedback, stakeholders are forced to resort to other 
pathways to get PJM’s attention. Comments during stakeholder meetings, side conversations in 
 
22 See e.g. Hybrid Resources Market Model Selection, Issue Charge, https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mic/2026/20260805/20260805-item-04-2---hybrid-resources-
market-model-selection---issue-charge.pdf.  
23 Pre-filed Statement of Susan Bruce, Counsel for PJM Industrial Customer Coalition at 17 (“PJM ICC 
Comments”).

9 
 
the hallways of Valley Forge, and unpublished emails to PJM staff should not be how PJM 
works with stakeholders to answer questions about its proposals and modify proposals to address 
legitimate stakeholder concerns. These pathways lack clarity and transparency. It also prevents 
PJM from hearing from critical voices that may not be able to be in the hallways during the 
plethora of  meetings.  
While focusing stakeholder discussions, PJM should provide opportunities to provide 
written feedback on its proposals. PJM does, sometimes, provide for the opportunity to submit 
written feedback, however, these requests for feedback are often late in the process and 
comments are not always posted publicly. Further, there is little formality to the process, leaving 
stakeholders to guess as to when, or even if, PJM will accept written feedback. MAREC Action 
and SEIA recommend that PJM establish stakeholder feedback processes like those of the 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) and the California Independent System 
Operator, Corp. (CAISO). Both MISO and CAISO have dedicated pages on their websites where 
stakeholders can submit written feedback and ask clarifying questions.24 Both MISO and CAISO 
provide written responses to that feedback. And both MISO and CAISO seek out that feedback 
early and often in the stakeholder process, allowing them to acknowledge where there are gaps in 
their understanding.  
In providing for written feedback, PJM can hear from, and respond to, voices that may be 
drowned out during stakeholder meetings. Further, it allows stakeholders to coordinate with each 
other and find common ground on proposals, ultimately leading to more supported proposals. 
 
 
24 See e.g. MISO, LLWG: Generation and Large Load Alignment, Stakeholder Feedback, 
https://www.misoenergy.org/engage/stakeholder-feedback/2026/llwg-generation-and-large-load-alignment-llwg-
2026-6-20260716/; see also CAISO Initiative: Day-ahead market enhancements, 
https://stakeholdercenter.caiso.com/StakeholderInitiatives/Day-ahead-market-enhancements.

10 
 
C. 
Improvements to polling: 
Because MAREC Action and SEIA are recommending that PJM consider moving to an 
advisory voting structure, the remaining recommendations in this section reflect changes to the 
polling process to allow PJM to gain more insight into the potential market impact on their tariff 
proposals. 
1. 
Recommendation: Throughout the process, PJM should conduct 
polling on specific elements of its proposals. 
In addition to gaining critical input through written comments, PJM should seek input on 
individual elements of a proposal, and should do so early and often throughout the stakeholder 
process. Polling reports should be divided out by sector and by business type. Voting on entire 
proposals could result in situations in which small, but impactful elements of a proposal are 
voted down because they are attached to a proposal that has elements that are unworkable to 
certain market participants. Polling specific elements of a proposal will allow PJM to understand 
what changes are necessary to develop a more supportive, and therefore more successful, 
proposal. 
2. 
Recommendation: When polling members, PJM should reflect poll 
results with more granularity.  
MAREC Action and SEIA’s member companies participate in PJM as generation 
developers. Generation developers are spread between two different sectors: the Generation 
Owner sector and the Other Supplier sector. This split is because the Operating Agreement 
differentiates between incumbent resource owners, which are part of the Generation Owner

11 
 
sector,25 and non-incumbent resource owners, which are relegated to the Other Supplier sector.26 
The Other Supplier sector also serves as a catch-all sector, serving as the sector for any company 
that does not fit within the requirements of the other sectors.27 Not only does this sector include 
non-incumbent generation developers, it includes financiers, power marketers, demand response 
aggregators, and consultants that specialize in representing wholesale market participants.28 
While PSEG is technically correct when it notes that “the Generation Owner and Other Supplier 
sectors had less than half of their membership in attendance” at the most recent CIFP for Large 
Loads,29 the statement failed to consider that such a small percentage of the sectors voted in the 
recent CIFP because the proposal is likely only relevant to that small percentage. 
 
PSEG’s statement reveals an underlying problem with the current sector structure: The 
sectors no longer reflect the diversity of stakeholders in PJM. This is not surprising. The sectors 
were established more than 25 years ago, as part of PJM’s Order No. 2000 compliance filing.30 
And the qualifications for the sectors have not changed since. Over that time, PJM has shifted 
greatly. More independent power producers entered the market. Developers shifted from coal to 
gas to renewables. Distributed resources gained access to the wholesale markets.31 Large 
customers are shifting from traditional manufacturing to data centers that are both larger and 
 
25 PJM Operating Agreement, Sec. 1, Definitions (defining Generator Owner as a resource shall have cleared an 
RPM auction and has a Commission-jurisdictional interconnection agreement or wholesale market participation 
agreement.) 
26 PJM Operating Agreement, Sec. 1, Definitions (defining “Other Supplier” as a member that “(i) is engaged in 
buying, selling or transmitting electric energy, capacity, ancillary services, financial transmission rights or other 
services available under PJM's governing documents in or through the Interconnection or has a good faith intent to 
do so, and” (ii) is not otherwise part of another sector.) 
27 Id.  
28 https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/member-services/membership-enrollment/full-member-enrollment  
29 PSEG Comments at 8. 
30 Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland Interconnection, 81 FERC ¶ 61,257, 62,262 (1997) (“The Members 
Committee will consist of 5 sectors representing generation owners, other suppliers, transmission owners, electric 
distributors, and end-use customers.”) 
31 Participation of Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations in Markets Operated by Regional Transmission 
Organizations and Independent System Operators, 172 FERC ¶ 61,247 (2020) (“Order No. 2222”).

12 
 
have different load profiles. The current sector structure never contemplated these market shifts 
and as a result, votes today do not tell the whole story of the industry impacts of a tariff change. 
 
For PJM to get a better understanding of the impacts of its proposals, MAREC Action 
and SEIA recommend that, as PJM conducts polls, which again, should be early and often, PJM 
should reflect not just the sectors in the polls, but various lines of business as well. PJM does 
reflect the various lines of business in its voting reports, which are posted several days after the 
vote is conducted,32 but because these votes are conducted so late in the process, the voting 
results do little to provide PJM with any insights into what changes need to be made to the 
proposal to address industry concerns. Further, recent polls show that PJM does not delineate 
between lines of business.33 In order to reflect the lines of business in polling, MAREC Action 
and SEIA recommend that PJM adopt the categories of lines of business reflected in the voting 
reports.34 
 
MAREC Action and SEIA do not recommend that PJM revise the Operating Agreement 
to redefine the sectors, as more research would be necessary to fully define those sectors. Such a 
change is not necessary for PJM to modify its polling to capture and reflect industry feedback in 
a way that provides a better understanding of the impacts of its proposals.  
  
 
32 See e.g. PJM Members Committee, Voting Results, Connect and Manage, at 6 (June 30, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260630-special/mc-voting-
results---agenda-item-3a---pjm-cm-proposal.pdf (showing the voting results broken down by line of business in 
PJM).  
33 See PJM, Governance and Stakeholder Process Poll Results (Aug. 12, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260819/20260819-item-10---1-governance-and-
stakeholder-process-poll-results.pdf; see also PJM, CIFP - Reliability Backstop Procurement / Connect & Manage 
Summarized Poll Results (July 16, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-
rbp/postings/cifp-poll-results-with-comments.pdf.  
34 See PJM Members Committee, Voting Results, Connect and Manage, at 6 (June 30, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260630-special/mc-voting-results---agenda-item-3a---
pjm-cm-proposal.pdf (reflecting the following lines of business: Ancillary Service Provider, Consumer Advocate, 
Curtailment Provider, Financial Trader, Industrial Customer, IOU, IPP, Project Developer, Public Power, Retail 
Marketer, and Wholesale Marketer).

13 
 
IV. 
Strengthening State Participation in the PJM Stakeholder Process 
State retail regulators have a statutory responsibility to ensure resource adequacy at the 
lowest reasonable cost and are directly accountable to consumers for retail electricity rates. Yet 
many of the rules governing resource adequacy are developed through the PJM stakeholder 
process, in which state regulators lack a formal role sufficient to effectively advance and 
implement their solutions. This disconnect between state responsibility and stakeholder authority 
should be addressed by strengthening the states’ role in PJM governance. 
MAREC and SEIA support reforms that would provide states, through OPSI, with a more 
meaningful and actionable voice in the PJM stakeholder process. Specifically, PJM Transmission 
Owners should make Section 205 filings on OPSI’s behalf when OPSI reaches consensus on cost 
allocation methods for regional transmission projects. In addition, if PJM is given authority to 
make unilateral Section 205 filings, PJM should also be required to make filings on OPSI’s 
behalf regarding regional transmission planning.  
These changes would better align PJM’s governance structure with practices already in 
place in other RTOs. More importantly, these changes recognize the states’ statutory 
responsibilities and ensure that the economic regulators accountable to retail consumers have a 
meaningful, effective, and actionable voice in the PJM decisions that directly affect them.

14 
 
V. 
Conclusion  
As the Commission, PJM, and stakeholders move through this dispute resolution process, 
MAREC and SEIA request that these recommendations are reflected in the reforms adopted in 
this proceeding.

Appendix: List of Recommendations 
Board Leadership and Transparency 
1. The Board and PJM should work with stakeholders to identify initiatives and develop an 
annual priorities plan. 
2. The Board should host open meetings, publish roll call votes, and issue decisional memos 
with their directives. 
3. Board members should schedule regular meetings with Members, States, and 
Stakeholders. 
Stakeholders voting rights 
4. Consider moving to an advisory voting system. 
Improvements to the Stakeholder Process 
5. At beginning of stakeholder process, PJM staff should establish the objectives any 
solution must satisfy and what solutions cannot be entertained. 
6. PJM should provide a pathway for written comments and questions on proposals that are 
publicly posted to a central location. 
7. Throughout the process, PJM should conduct polling on specific elements of its 
proposals. 
8. When polling members, PJM should reflect poll results with more granularity.
